Estimate impulse responses via heteroskedasticity-based IV local projections

Source: R/hetiv.R
hetiv.Rd

Estimates impulse response functions (IRFs) using recursive heteroskedasticity-IV identification (Rigobon, 2003; Rigobon and Sack, 2004; Lewis, 2022; Burri and Kaufmann, 2026a, 2026b) combined with local projections (Jorda, 2005). Identification exploits the difference in variance between policy event days and control days to construct instruments for the endogenous variables. It also returns weak instrument tests as well as shock predictions on event days.

Usage

hetiv(
  y,
  O,
  X = NULL,
  Ind,
  P,
  H,
  E = 1,
  norm = 1,
  interact = FALSE,
  cum = FALSE,
  cov_type = "HC3",
  hpredict = 0,
  pooled = FALSE,
  details = FALSE
)

Arguments

y

Numeric matrix of outcome variables (T x N). The effect on the first variable in each dimension is normalized to unity at horizon 0. These variables are also used to construct heteroskedasticity-based instruments and for recursive ordering to identify multiple dimensions.

O

Numeric matrix of information set variables (T x M). Should include at least y in case of non-stationary variables. Included as lags 1 through P.

X

Numeric matrix of deterministic variables (T x K). For example, time trend, seasonal dummies or other deterministic controls. Included as is (no lags). A constant is included by default.

Ind

Integer vector of length T, event indicator:

  • 0 Control day (no event)

  • 1 Policy day (event)

  • 2 Contaminated control day (excluded from estimation)

P

Integer. Maximum lag order for the information set. Set to 0 for no lags (regression on deterministic terms only).

H

Integer. Maximum horizon (in periods) up to which IRFs are estimated.

E

Integer. Number of shock dimensions to identify via recursive ordering.

norm

Numeric scalar. Normalize the impact response of the first variable to a specific value. Defaults to 1 for standard unit-effect normalization.

interact

Logical. If TRUE, lagged information set variables are interacted with event/non-event dummies.

cum

Logical vector of length N. For each variable in y, whether to report the cumulative impulse response instead of the level response. If only one provided, applied to all impulse responses.

cov_type

Covariance estimator for local-projection standard errors: "HC3" (default) for heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors or "NW" for Newey-West HAC standard errors. "HC3" is the default because Montiel Olea et al. (2025) show that heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors suffice for local-projection impulse responses under weak conditions, even though multi-step forecast errors are typically serially correlated. "NW" remains available as an optional HAC robustness check.

hpredict

Integer. Horizon of the responses and forecast errors used for shock prediction, on the same scale as the row labels of irf. Defaults to 0 (recommended; impact response and one-step-ahead residual are used) Must lie between 0 and H - 1.

pooled

Logical. If FALSE (default), the shock prediction uses the forecast errors and responses at horizon hpredict only. If TRUE, the forecast errors of all horizons 0, ..., hpredict are stacked and used jointly (pooled prediction); see kfpredict(). With hpredict = 0 both options coincide.

details

Logical. If TRUE, saves detailed IV results, weak instrument tests, and shock prediction results, which is slightly slower. If FALSE, returns only impulse responses and standard errors.

Value

A named list. Always contains:

irf

Array (H x N x E) of estimated impulse responses.

se

Array (H x N x E) of local-projection standard errors.

Method

Character string "Heteroskedasticity-IV".

With details = TRUE, additionally contains:

irf

Array (H x N x E) of estimated impulse responses.

se

Array (H x N x E) of local-projection standard errors.

Shocks

Predicted structural shocks on event days from kfpredict(), based on the responses at horizon hpredict.

IVRes

List of ivreg model objects, one per horizon, variable, and shock dimension.

OLSRes

List of the information-set regressions whose residuals enter the shock prediction, named OLS.n<i>.h<h> by outcome variable and horizon.

ORTHRes

List of OLS models used to orthogonalize the variable underlying the instrument, one per shock dimension.

FirstStage

For E = 1: data frame with one row per horizon h giving the number of observations Tobs, the homoskedastic first-stage F statistic F_hom (the squared t statistic of the proxy; Stock and Yogo, 2005) and the robust effective F statistic F_rob of Montiel Olea and Pflueger (2013), always computed with the HAC (Newey-West) covariance estimator, irrespective of cov_type. The statistics do not depend on the outcome variable. NULL for E > 1.

WeakTest

For E > 1: data frame with one row per shock dimension target (e = 1, ..., E), horizon h and outcome variable i, giving the results of gweakivtest() for the system with the first e policy variables as endogenous regressors and the first e instruments as instruments, targeting the coefficient on policy variable e: Tobs, gmin (generalized minimum eigenvalue statistic, which depends on the horizon only through the sample), cv and cv_simplified (sharp and simplified critical values, which may depend on the outcome and horizon), and the Stock-Yogo statistic sy_stat with its critical value sy_cv (NaN unless over-identified). The test always uses the HAC (Newey-West) covariance estimator, irrespective of cov_type, and the relative bias criterion (crit = "rel"), for comparability with Montiel Olea and Pflueger (2013). Rows where the outcome is a policy variable (i <= E) on impact are omitted. NULL for E = 1.

Obs

Data frame with observation counts: Tp (policy days), Tc (control days), To (contaminated days), Tt (total used).

Method

Character string "Heteroskedasticity-IV".

et

Data frame of forecast errors on event days used for shock prediction: residuals of the regression of y_{t+h} on the information set dated t - 1, one column per variable and horizon (y1.h0, ..., yN.h0, y1.h1, ...). One horizon (hpredict) if pooled = FALSE, horizons 0, ..., hpredict if pooled = TRUE.

Sig

Covariance matrix of et on event days.

SigR

Covariance matrix of the same residuals on control days, or NA if unavailable. A control day enters horizon h only if no event occurs in its window t + 1, ..., t + h.

Psi

Response matrix used for shock prediction, with rows matching the columns of et: irf[hpredict + 1, , ] (N x E) if pooled = FALSE, the rows 1, ..., hpredict + 1 of irf stacked (N(hpredict + 1) x E) if pooled = TRUE. With the default hpredict = 0 this is the impact response.

WeakData

Data frame of endogenous variables and instruments for the Lewis-Mertens (2025) weak instrument test.

Details

For E > 1, identification is recursive and order-dependent: the column order of y defines both the shock ordering and the normalization variable for each shock dimension.

References

Burri, M. and D. Kaufmann (2026a). Measuring monetary policy shocks. IRENE Working Papers 24-03, IRENE Institute of Economic Research, University of Neuchatel.

Burri, M. and D. Kaufmann (2026b). Multiple monetary policy shocks from daily data: A heteroskedasticity IV approach. Economics Letters, 268, 113091. doi:10.1016/j.econlet.2026.113091

Jorda, O. (2005). Estimation and inference of impulse responses by local projections. American Economic Review, 95(1), 161-182.

Lewis, D. J. (2022). Robust inference in models identified via heteroskedasticity. Review of Economics and Statistics, 104(3), 510-524.

Lewis, D. J. and Mertens, K. (2025). A robust test for weak instruments for 2SLS with multiple endogenous regressors. Review of Economic Studies, DOI: 10.1093/restud/rdaf103

Montiel Olea, J. L., M. Plagborg-Moller, E. Qian, and C. K. Wolf (2025). Local projections or VARs? A primer for macroeconomists. NBER Working Paper No. 33871.

Rigobon, R. (2003). Identification through heteroskedasticity. Review of Economics and Statistics, 85(4), 777-792.

Rigobon, R. and Sack, B. (2004). The impact of monetary policy on asset prices. Journal of Monetary Economics, 51(8), 1553-1575.

Examples

set.seed(1)
y <- matrix(rnorm(80), ncol = 2)
Ind <- rep(0L, nrow(y))
Ind[seq(5, nrow(y), by = 5)] <- 1L
res <- hetiv(y = y, O = y, Ind = Ind, P = 1, H = 3, details = TRUE)
#> Warning: Some estimated shock variances are negative (weak heteroskedasticity); using absolute values for scaling.
dim(res$irf)
#> [1] 3 2 1
